texts.title: Drawing depth on a flat wall

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has tried to draw a street or a room knows how quickly the result begins to look wrong. Walls that should run away from the viewer lean at odd angles, people at the back of a scene seem as large as those at the front, and floors tilt upwards as though they were about to slide their contents out of the picture. For most of the history of painting, artists dealt with these problems by instinct and convention rather than by rule. The results could be charming, but they rarely convinced the eye. Many cultures produced great art without ever wanting to solve these problems at all. The system known as linear perspective, which gives a flat surface the appearance of depth by following strict geometric rules, is a comparatively recent invention.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Painters before it were not ignorant of depth. Wall paintings from the ancient Mediterranean show buildings whose edges recede convincingly, and artists in several traditions placed distant figures higher up the picture to suggest that they were further away. What such images lacked was consistency. Lines that should meet at a single point instead converge on several, so that each part of a picture may be convincing on its own while the whole does not describe one coherent space. In some traditions this was a deliberate choice: in many East Asian landscape scrolls, the viewer is invited to travel through the picture rather than to stand at one fixed spot, and a single viewpoint would have defeated the purpose.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The rules that made consistency possible were worked out in Italy early in the fifteenth century. According to an account written a generation later, an architect demonstrated them with a small painted panel showing a church and the square in front of it, in which he had drilled a hole. The viewer stood behind the panel, looked through the hole at a mirror held in front of it, and saw the painting reflected in exactly the position that the real building occupied; lowering the mirror revealed the real square, which matched the image. The demonstration was, in effect, a proof. Whether the experiment happened quite as described is uncertain, since the panel has not survived, but the principle it illustrated was soon written down in a treatise on painting and spread rapidly through the workshops of the time.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The core of that principle is simple to state. Lines that run parallel in the real world and lead away from the viewer are drawn so that they meet at one point on the horizon, called the vanishing point, and objects shrink in a fixed proportion as they move towards it. A painter who knows the height of a figure at the front of a scene can therefore calculate exactly how tall an identical figure should be at any given distance. Nothing in the rule depends on talent. For the first time, the size of things in a picture was governed by measurement rather than by their importance, and a king at the back of a crowd had to be drawn smaller than a servant standing in front of it.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: This new precision came at a price, and not every artist was willing to pay it. A perspective drawing is correct from only one position, the point from which the picture was constructed, and seen from anywhere else it is subtly distorted. Painters of large ceilings and walls, which would be seen from many angles by people walking beneath them, often bent the rules deliberately, and some produced effects that only work when the viewer stands on a spot marked on the floor. Others found the system too rigid for the subjects they cared about: a scene built entirely from straight lines and measured distances could look more like an architectural diagram than a living world.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Perspective also changed what painters needed to know. Workshops that had trained apprentices by having them copy their masters’ designs now had to teach geometry, and a number of the most influential painters of the following century wrote books on the subject, several of them illustrated with elaborate constructions of many-sided solids and vaulted halls. The skills overlapped increasingly with those of architects and engineers, and the same kind of diagram could be used to plan a building, design a stage set or map a fortification. For a time, knowledge of perspective was one of the marks that separated a painter who was regarded as learned from one who was regarded as a mere craftsman.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Some historians have argued that linear perspective was more than a technique, and that it expressed a new way of thinking in which the world was something to be measured from the standpoint of an individual observer. Others regard this claim as too neat, pointing out that medieval scholars had already studied optics in detail and that many painters used perspective loosely, or not at all, for centuries afterwards. What is not disputed is its durability. Photography, which records light passing through a lens onto a flat surface, produces images that obey the same geometry automatically, and the computer graphics used in films and games today rely on calculations that painters once worked out with a ruler and a length of string.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: At the beginning of the twentieth century, almost every large city in Europe and North America, and many in South America, Asia and Australia, had a network of electric trams. They were the first form of mechanised transport that ordinary workers could afford to use every day, and they shaped cities as decisively as railways had shaped countries: new districts grew up along the lines, and the distance a family could live from its place of work was set largely by how far the tram would carry them in half an hour. Some lines were even laid across open fields, in the expectation that houses would follow. Fifty years later, in much of the English-speaking world and in parts of Europe, the networks had almost entirely disappeared.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The usual explanation for that disappearance is the private car, but the history is more complicated. Many tram companies were private businesses operating under agreements that fixed their fares for decades, and when wages and the price of materials rose after the First World War, they could no longer afford to maintain their tracks. Worn rails made for slow, noisy journeys, which drove passengers away and reduced income further. Many companies simply went bankrupt. Motor buses, which needed no track and could be moved to new routes overnight, offered city authorities a way out: the cost of the road they used was paid by the public as a whole rather than by the operator, whereas a tram company paid for every metre of its own line.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: There was also a question of who the street belonged to. Trams ran along the middle of the road, and passengers had to cross traffic to reach them. As the number of private cars grew, drivers and the organisations that represented them increasingly described the tram as an obstacle, and the engineers who planned roads in the middle decades of the century tended to measure success by how many vehicles a street could move rather than how many people. Every metre given to rails was a metre that could not be used for parking. By that measure the tram, which occupied road space that cars could otherwise use, looked like a waste, even though a single full tram carried as many passengers as dozens of cars.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Not every country followed the same path. In much of central and eastern Europe, and in several cities in the Netherlands, Switzerland and Germany, networks were kept and gradually modernised, often because they were publicly owned and not expected to make a profit, and sometimes simply because there was not enough money to replace them with anything else. Some of these cities never stopped building new lines, even in the decades when others were tearing theirs up. These systems later became the models for the revival: they showed that trams given their own lanes and priority at traffic lights could be almost as fast as an underground railway, at a fraction of the cost of tunnelling.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: That revival began in the late 1970s and gathered pace in the 1990s, when a number of cities that had removed their trams a generation earlier started to build new lines. A few of the new lines even followed routes that had closed half a century before. The vehicles were different from their predecessors: low floors allowed passengers with prams and wheelchairs to board without climbing steps, and they were longer, quieter and faster than the old cars. The motives were different too. Planners valued the tram not only as a means of moving people but as a way of changing the character of a street, and several French cities used new lines as an opportunity to replace car lanes with wide pavements, rows of trees and grass laid between the rails.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The revival has its critics. A tram line costs far more to build than a bus route, and the construction period, often several years of closed roads and diverted traffic, can do lasting harm to shops along the route. Some transport economists argue that the same money spent on buses running in dedicated lanes would carry more passengers over a wider area. They also note that a tram cannot overtake a broken-down vehicle in front of it. Supporters reply that the comparison misses the point: the permanence of rails, they say, persuades developers and residents that a service will still be there in twenty years, and this confidence attracts investment in housing and offices along the route in a way that a bus lane, which can be removed by the next council, rarely does.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Evidence for that claim is mixed. Property values near new tram stops have risen in many cities, but it is difficult to separate the effect of the line from other changes happening at the same time, and in some cases the line was deliberately built through areas where development was already planned. What is clearer is that the tram’s return has been driven less by transport arithmetic than by a change in what cities want their streets to be for. The vehicle that was removed to make room for cars has come back, in many places, as part of an effort to take room away from them.
paragraphs.label: G

texts.title: Should the referee trust the replay?

paragraphs.text: For most of the history of professional sport, the decision of the referee was final in a literal sense: whatever the official saw, or thought he saw, became the truth of the match. Television gradually changed that. Once millions of viewers could watch a disputed moment again from several angles, often before the players had returned to their positions, it became hard to defend a system in which the one person without access to the replay was the one who had to decide. Officials themselves, it is worth saying, were often among those asking for help. Over the past two decades almost every major sport has introduced some form of video review, and the question is no longer whether technology should be used but how far it should go.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: In sports where the question to be answered is purely factual, the case is hard to argue with. Whether a ball crossed a line or landed inside a court can be measured by cameras more accurately than by any human eye, and systems that do this have been accepted with remarkably little fuss. In tennis, the result has been a clear improvement, and nobody now argues for going back. The sports scientist Elena Varga, who has studied line-calling in tennis, found that umpires were wrong on around one close call in twelve before automated systems were adopted. Players now accept the machine’s verdict almost without protest, partly because it is delivered instantly and partly because it leaves no room for suspicion that an official favoured one side.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The difficulty begins where the decision is not a matter of fact but of judgement. Whether a tackle was reckless or a player was deliberately obstructed cannot be measured by a camera; it has to be interpreted, and slowing the footage down can make ordinary contact look violent. Two experienced officials watching the same clip can disagree, and frequently do. The former referee Samuel Adeyemi argues that video reviews of such incidents do not remove human error but relocate it, from an official on the field who saw the incident at full speed to another in a studio who sees it frozen. In his experience the second decision is not reliably better than the first; it is merely made with more confidence.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: There is also the matter of time. A football match used to flow for long stretches, and supporters in the stadium experienced the game at the same moment as the players. Reviews interrupt that flow, sometimes for several minutes, and those in the stadium often have no idea what is being checked. The noise that follows a goal is now often postponed, and sometimes cancelled altogether. Research by the economist Hannah Brook on attendance figures found no clear evidence that reviews had driven spectators away, but surveys of supporters regularly show that the delay before a goal can be celebrated is among the changes they dislike most. I suspect this dislike is not trivial, because the spontaneity of a crowd’s reaction is part of what spectators are paying for.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Defenders of video review reply that fairness matters more than atmosphere, and that a result decided by an obvious error is worse than a celebration postponed by a minute. This is persuasive for the kind of blatant mistake that everyone watching at home can see immediately. It is much less persuasive for the marginal decisions that reviews now routinely reopen, such as whether an attacker’s shoulder was a few centimetres beyond a defender. Here technology offers a precision that the rules were never written to require, and it has produced decisions that are correct according to the lines drawn on the screen but seem absurd to almost everyone who watches them. No one ever bought a ticket to watch a line being drawn.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Some sports have responded by limiting how the technology is used. In several, a review can only be requested by the teams themselves, who are given a small number of challenges per match and lose one each time they are wrong; others have instructed officials to overturn a decision only when the error is clear and obvious. The sociologist Marta Lind, who has compared these approaches, argues that challenge systems work better because they give responsibility back to the participants and turn each review into a dramatic event in its own right rather than an unexplained pause. Where challenges have been introduced, complaints about reviews appear to have become less frequent.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: My own view is that the debate has been framed wrongly. Video review was introduced to prevent injustice, and it is excellent at settling questions of fact. The trouble has come from asking it to settle questions of interpretation, where there is no single correct answer to be found, and from treating the smallest measurable margin as though it were the same thing as fairness. Sport is a contest between people, judged by people, and a degree of human error is part of what makes it recognisable. A match without controversy would also be a match with very little to talk about afterwards. The aim should be to remove the mistakes that make a result unjust, not every mistake that a camera happens to be capable of finding.
paragraphs.label: G

explanation.ru: Абзац C: один полный трамвай везёт столько же, сколько десятки машин → C.

items.quote: sometimes simply because there was not enough money to replace them with anything else
items.prompt: a reason why some systems were kept simply because of a shortage of funds

explanation.en: Paragraph D: some networks survived because there was no money to replace them → D. Paragraph B is about lacking money for repairs, which caused decline.
explanation.kk: D абзацы: кейде желіні ауыстыруға ақша жетпегендіктен қалдырған → D. B абзацында ақша жолды жөндеуге жетпеген — бұл сақталудың емес, құлдыраудың себебі.
explanation.ru: Абзац D: иногда сети оставляли, потому что не было денег их чем-то заменить → D. В B речь о нехватке денег на ремонт путей — это причина упадка, а не сохранения.

items.quote: the distance a family could live from its place of work was set largely by how far the tram would carry them in half an hour
items.prompt: a description of how trams affected where families could afford to settle

explanation.en: Paragraph A: how far families could live from work depended on the tram’s half-hour range → A. Paragraph F mentions housing only as investment.
explanation.kk: A абзацы: отбасы жұмыстан қаншалықты алыс тұра алатынын жарты сағаттық трамвай жолы шешкен → A. F абзацында тұрғын үй бар, бірақ инвестиция ретінде.
explanation.ru: Абзац A: насколько далеко от работы могла жить семья, решал трамвай за полчаса → A. В F говорится о жилье вдоль линий, но как об инвестициях, а не о выборе семей.

items.quote: it is difficult to separate the effect of the line from other changes happening at the same time
items.prompt: a reference to the difficulty of proving that a new line raised the price of property

explanation.en: Paragraph G: it is hard to separate the line’s effect from other changes → G.
explanation.kk: G абзацы: желінің әсерін басқа өзгерістерден ажырату қиын → G.
explanation.ru: Абзац G: трудно отделить влияние линии от других перемен → G.

items.quote: can do lasting harm to shops along the route
items.prompt: a mention of the damage that construction can cause to local businesses

explanation.en: Paragraph F: years of closed roads harm shops along the route → F.
explanation.kk: F абзацы: көшелер жабылған бірнеше жылдық құрылыс бағыт бойындағы дүкендерге зиян келтіреді → F.
explanation.ru: Абзац F: годы стройки с перекрытыми улицами вредят магазинам вдоль линии → F.

groups.instruction: Text 2 has seven paragraphs, A–G. Which paragraph contains the following information? Write the correct letter, A–G.

items.quote: systems that do this have been accepted with remarkably little fuss
items.prompt: Players have been slow to accept automated line-calling.

explanation.en: “accepted with remarkably little fuss”, “almost without protest” → NO.
explanation.kk: «accepted with remarkably little fuss»; ойыншылар шешімді «almost without protest» қабылдайды → NO.
explanation.ru: «accepted with remarkably little fuss» и игроки принимают вердикт «almost without protest» → NO.

items.quote: slowing the footage down can make ordinary contact look violent
items.prompt: Watching a challenge in slow motion shows more accurately how dangerous it was.

explanation.en: “slowing the footage down can make ordinary contact look violent” → NO.
explanation.kk: «slowing the footage down can make ordinary contact look violent» → NO: баяулатылған қайталау дәлдемейді, бұрмалайды.
explanation.ru: «slowing the footage down can make ordinary contact look violent» → NO: замедленный повтор искажает, а не уточняет.

items.quote: Reviews interrupt that flow, sometimes for several minutes
items.prompt: Reviews in football take longer on average than in other sports.

explanation.en: Football reviews can last several minutes, but there is no comparison with other sports → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Футболда үзіліс бірнеше минутқа созылатыны айтылған, бірақ басқа спорт түрлерімен салыстыру жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Сказано, что в футболе пауза бывает несколько минут, но сравнения с другими видами спорта нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: surveys of supporters regularly show that the delay before a goal can be celebrated is among the changes they dislike most
items.prompt: Fans watching on television dislike reviews more than those inside the stadium.

explanation.en: Surveys show fans dislike the delay before celebrating, but TV viewers and stadium crowds are never compared → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Сауалнама жанкүйерлер гол алдындағы кідірісті ұнатпайтынын көрсетеді. Теледидар алдындағылар мен стадиондағыларды салыстыру жоқ → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Опросы говорят, что болельщики не любят задержку перед празднованием гола. Сравнения зрителей у телевизора и на стадионе нет → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: who are given a small number of challenges per match and lose one each time they are wrong
items.prompt: Teams using challenge systems win more matches when they make fewer challenges.

explanation.en: The challenge system is described, but no link between challenges and winning is mentioned → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.kk: Шақыру жүйесі сипатталған (қателессе, команда шақыруынан айырылады), бірақ шақыру саны мен жеңістің байланысы айтылмаған → NOT GIVEN.
explanation.ru: Описано устройство системы вызовов (команда теряет вызов при ошибке), но о связи числа вызовов с победами — ничего → NOT GIVEN.

items.quote: a degree of human error is part of what makes it recognisable
items.prompt: Some officiating mistakes should be accepted as part of sport.

explanation.en: “a degree of human error is part of what makes it recognisable” → YES.
explanation.kk: «a degree of human error is part of what makes it recognisable»; тек нәтижені әділетсіз ететін қателерді жою керек → YES.
explanation.ru: «a degree of human error is part of what makes it recognisable»; убирать нужно лишь ошибки, делающие результат несправедливым → YES.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Text 3? Write YES if the statement agrees with the claims of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the claims of the writer, NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

items.quote: do not remove human error but relocate it
items.prompt: Using replays shifts mistakes to a different person rather than eliminating them.

explanation.en: Adeyemi: reviews “do not remove human error but relocate it” → B.
explanation.kk: Adeyemi: қайталау «do not remove human error but relocate it» — алаңдағы төрешіден студиядағыға → B.
explanation.ru: Adeyemi: повторы «do not remove human error but relocate it» — от судьи на поле к судье в студии → B.

items.quote: umpires were wrong on around one close call in twelve
items.prompt: Before machines were used, officials misjudged a notable share of close calls.

explanation.en: Varga: umpires were wrong on about one close call in twelve → A.
explanation.kk: Varga: төрешілер он екі даулы жағдайдың шамамен біреуінде қателескен → A.
explanation.ru: Varga: судьи ошибались примерно в одном спорном случае из двенадцати → A.

items.quote: turn each review into a dramatic event in its own right
items.prompt: Allowing competitors to ask for a review makes each one more engaging.

explanation.en: Lind: challenges return responsibility to players and make each review “a dramatic event” → D.
explanation.kk: Lind: шақыру жүйесі жауапкершілікті қатысушыларға қайтарып, тексеруді «dramatic event»-ке айналдырады → D.
explanation.ru: Lind: система вызовов возвращает ответственность участникам и превращает проверку в «dramatic event» → D.

items.quote: found no clear evidence that reviews had driven spectators away
items.prompt: Figures on crowd sizes fail to prove that reviews have reduced attendance.

explanation.en: Brook: attendance figures show no clear loss of spectators → C. Dislike of the delay comes from fan surveys, not her study.
explanation.kk: Brook: келушілер туралы дерек көрермен азайғанын көрсетпейді → C. Кідіріске наразылық — оның зерттеуінен емес, жанкүйерлер сауалнамасынан.
explanation.ru: Brook: данные о посещаемости не показывают, что зрители ушли → C. Недовольство задержкой — из опросов болельщиков, а не из её исследования.

Hannah Brook

groups.instruction: Look at the following statements and the list of people below. Match each statement with the correct person, A–D.

items.quote: In sports where the question to be answered is purely factual, the case is hard to argue with.
items.prompt: questions that are purely 37 ____

explanation.en: “the question to be answered is purely factual” → factual.
explanation.kk: «the question to be answered is purely factual» → factual.
explanation.ru: «the question to be answered is purely factual» → factual.

items.quote: The difficulty begins where the decision is not a matter of fact but of judgement.
items.prompt: decisions that call for 38 ____

explanation.en: “not a matter of fact but of judgement” → judgement (judgment also accepted).
explanation.kk: «not a matter of fact but of judgement» → judgement (judgment емлесі де есептеледі). «interpretation» келмейді.
explanation.ru: «not a matter of fact but of judgement» → judgement (американское написание judgment тоже засчитывается). «interpretation» не подходит: пропуск стоит до слова «interpreted».

items.quote: technology offers a precision that the rules were never written to require
items.prompt: introduces a 39 ____

explanation.en: “technology offers a precision that the rules were never written to require” → precision.
explanation.kk: «technology offers a precision that the rules were never written to require» → precision.
explanation.ru: «technology offers a precision that the rules were never written to require» → precision.

items.quote: overturn a decision only when the error is clear and obvious
items.prompt: clear and 40 ____

explanation.en: “overturn a decision only when the error is clear and obvious” → obvious.
explanation.kk: «overturn a decision only when the error is clear and obvious» → obvious.
explanation.ru: «overturn a decision only when the error is clear and obvious» → obvious.
